analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal-state process to review and block unreasonable health insurance premium increases.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 13 Senate sponsors but never left the Senate health committee; it died without any vote when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health insurers to justify premium increases before putting them into effect, and allowed federal or state regulators to deny, reduce, or rebate increases they found unreasonable. It would have created a seven-member Health Insurance Rate Authority to advise regulators, set up a public database of rate increases and insurer justifications, and sent states $250 million in grants to do the reviews. In states that could not or would not review rates, the federal government would have done it instead.
analysis.who_benefits: People and small businesses buying health insurance, especially in the individual and small-group markets where premiums were rising fastest, gain from prior review of rate increases, public disclosure of insurer justifications, and possible rebates when an increase is found unreasonable [S3]. States gain grant money and federal help building rate-review capacity [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurance customers, especially individuals and small employers

how_it_helps.text: Insurers must submit a justification for a potentially unreasonable rate increase before it takes effect and post it publicly on their websites, with the Secretary ensuring public disclosure for all issuers [S3].

Regulators can deny, modify, or order rebates for increases found unreasonable, with priority given to increases affecting large numbers of consumers and to the individual and small-group markets [S3].

A Health Insurance Rate Authority of seven members, including at least two consumer advocates, advises the Secretary, and an annual public report tracks rate increases state by state and insurer by insurer [S3].
States receive grants, up to $5 million per state per year from a $250 million authorization, to review rates and report trend data to the federal government [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance issuers bear the cost of prior justification, electronic reporting, public disclosure, possible denials or rebates of increases, and civil penalties for violations [S2] [S3]. Taxpayers fund the $250 million grant program and federal administrative costs [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill inserts the federal government into insurance rate regulation, which has historically been a state function; the Secretary decides which states keep control and which lose it, based on federal judgment of state capability [S2] [S3].

Reviewing premiums does not address the underlying cost of medical care; blocking an increase without changing underlying costs could squeeze insurers' ability to pay claims or lead them to reduce covered benefits or exit markets, and insurers argue many increases simply reflect rising medical costs [S3].

The bill authorizes $250 million in grants plus annual administrative spending, and the required NAIC report on a definition of 'unreasonable' was due just six months after enactment, a demanding timeline [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real but limited by design: rate review can stop unjustified increases and force disclosure, but it cannot by itself make care cheaper, and denying increases could cause insurers to narrow benefits or leave markets. The main cost is federal spending of roughly $250 million plus administration, and a shift of regulatory power from states toward Washington. On balance the bill targets a concrete pocketbook problem — double-digit premium increases with little accountability — with mechanisms that had worked in states that already reviewed rates.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on March 4, 2010, joined by Sens. Boxer, Whitehouse, Reed, and Sanders as original introducers [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S1] [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action; the bill never received a vote in either chamber [S5].
Twelve additional senators cosponsored the bill, all Democrats or the chamber's Independent, for 13 total sponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers came out ahead: they faced no federal rate-review process, no public justification requirement, and no possibility of rebates from this bill, since it never advanced. The Senate committee leaders who let it sit also avoided a fight over federalizing insurance regulation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, whose premiums faced no review

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors were Democrats plus the chamber's sole Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a recorded vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: Insurers would have had to justify premium increases before imposing them, post those justifications publicly, accept denial or modification of unreasonable increases, and possibly pay rebates and civil penalties [S2] [S3]. Because insurers profit from setting premiums without prior review, their interest in this bill ran against the consumers the bill was meant to protect.

States with rate-review authority could keep control and receive federal grants of up to $5 million per year; states judged unable to review rates would have that power taken over by the Secretary [S3]. The record does not show organized state support or opposition to the bill.
